question: A thymidine kinase-deficient varicella-zoster virus strain has been isolated at a retirement home. Many of the elderly had been infected with this strain and are experiencing shingles. Which of the following would be the best antiviral agent to treat this population?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Thymidine kinase-deficient varicella-zoster virus strain -> reduced susceptibility to acyclovir -> decreased efficacy of acyclovir in treating shingles in this population -> 80%

CHAIN: Thymidine kinase-deficient varicella-zoster virus strain -> potential cross-resistance to famciclovir due to similar mechanism of action as acyclovir -> limited effectiveness of famciclovir in treating shingles in this population -> 75%

CHAIN: Thymidine kinase-deficient varicella-zoster virus strain -> resistance to ganciclovir due to lack of thymidine kinase -> ganciclovir not recommended for treating shingles caused by this strain -> 90%

CHAIN: Thymidine kinase-deficient varicella-zoster virus strain -> no impact on cidofovir efficacy as it does not require viral thymidine kinase for activation -> potential consideration of cidofovir for treating shingles in this population -> 70%

CHAIN: Thymidine kinase-deficient varicella-zoster virus strain -> no direct effect on amantadine efficacy as it targets a different viral protein -> possible consideration of amantadine for treating shingles in this population -> 60%
analysis: Acyclovir is the best antiviral agent for treating varicella-zoster virus infections, including shingles, in the elderly population. It is the first-line treatment due to its efficacy and safety profile.
